title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text: Full lecture: CS229 Lecture 2 on YouTube (Stanford has disabled embedding, so it opens on YouTube). The video above is a shorter companion on the same idea.

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Key ideas
A linear hypothesis with x_0 = 1 for the intercept:

h_\theta(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{d} \theta_j x_j = \theta^\top x

The least-squares cost over n training examples:

J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)^2

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Gradient descent
Repeat until convergence, for every j at once:

\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}


Batch gradient descent uses all n examples per step: an exact gradient, but slow on large data.
Stochastic gradient descent updates after each example: noisy, but it starts making progress immediately.







TipLearning rate



If J(\theta) goes up between iterations, \alpha is too large. Try dividing it by about 3 each time.


import numpy as np

def batch_gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=0.01, iters=1000):
    """X: (n, d+1) with a leading column of ones; y: (n,)."""
    theta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        residual = X @ theta - y
        theta -= alpha * X.T @ residual / len(y)
    return theta

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Normal equations
Setting \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = 0 gives a closed form:

\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y

theta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)  # more stable than an explicit inverse

title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
Six functions









Item and key formula
Example
Application




1. Power x^nd/dx: n x^{n-1}\int: \tfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}, fails at n = -1
f = x^3 \to f' = 3x^2,\ \int = \tfrac{x^4}{4}\int_0^2 x^3\,dx = \tfrac{16}{4} = \mathbf{4}
Area and volume (x^2, x^3), cost curves, falling bodies (d = \tfrac12 g t^2), polynomial regression


2. Sine \sin xd/dx: \cos x\int: -\cos x
Slope at 0: \cos 0 = \mathbf{1}One arch: \int_0^\pi \sin x\,dx = [-\cos x]_0^\pi = \mathbf{2}
Anything that repeats: sound, AC electricity, vibration, seasonal or time-of-day demand


3. Cosine \cos xd/dx: -\sin x\int: \sin x
Slope at \pi/2: -\sin(\pi/2) = \mathbf{-1}\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos x\,dx = [\sin x]_0^{\pi/2} = \mathbf{1}
Same as sine (a shifted wave); oscillators, signal processing, Fourier analysis


4. Exponential e^{cx}d/dx: c\,e^{cx}\int: \tfrac{e^{cx}}{c}
f = e^{2x} \to f' = 2e^{2x} (growth proportional to size)\int_0^1 e^{2x}\,dx = \tfrac{e^2 - 1}{2} \approx \mathbf{3.19}
Population growth, compound interest, radioactive decay, drug clearance, exponential smoothing


5. Logarithm \ln xd/dx: \tfrac{1}{x}\int: x \ln x - x(\ln x fills the n = -1 gap)
Slope at x = 2: \mathbf{1/2}\int_1^e \ln x\,dx = [x \ln x - x]_1^e = 0 - (-1) = \mathbf{1}
Log scales (dB, pH, Richter), log-loss in ML, log-likelihood (turns products into sums)


6. Step0 for x < 0, 1 for x \ge 0d/dx: delta (spike, area 1)\int: ramp
A switch turning on at t = 0Ramp: \int_0^3 \text{step}\,dt = \mathbf{3}Delta: a sudden kick (hammer hit) with total area \mathbf{1}
Step: switch-on, policy change. Ramp: ReLU in neural nets, overtime cost past a threshold. Delta: impulse or one-time shock





Theorem formulation


1. Power
\frac{d}{dx}x^n = n\,x^{n-1}, \qquad \int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C







Part
Meaning




x
Input, the quantity that changes


n
Power: sets the shape of the curve


n\,x^{n-1}
Slope: the power comes down in front, then drops by one


\tfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}
Area: the power rises by one, then divides


n \ne -1
Needed for the area, since n = -1 divides by zero (\ln x takes over)


C
Any constant: its slope is 0, so the derivative cannot see it





2. Sine
\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x, \qquad \int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C







Part
Meaning




x
Angle in radians (the formulas fail in degrees)


\sin x
Height of the point at angle x on the unit circle


\cos x
Slope of the sine wave at x


-\cos x
Area so far; the minus sign is there because (\cos x)' = -\sin x





3. Cosine
\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x, \qquad \int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C







Part
Meaning




\cos x
Horizontal position on the unit circle; sine shifted by \pi/2


-\sin x
Slope: cosine starts at its peak, so it falls first


\sin x
Area under the cosine wave so far





4. Exponential
\frac{d}{dx}e^{cx} = c\,e^{cx}, \qquad \int e^{cx}\,dx = \frac{e^{cx}}{c} + C







Part
Meaning




e
The base (\approx 2.718) for which (e^x)' = e^x


c
Rate: growth if c > 0, decay if c < 0 (the area formula needs c \ne 0)


c\,e^{cx}
Slope: the rate times the current size


\tfrac{1}{c}
Undoes the factor c that differentiating brings out





5. Logarithm
\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad \int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C



Part
Meaning




\ln x
The power of e that gives x; needs x > 0


\tfrac{1}{x}
Slope: steep near 0, flatter as x grows


x \ln x
First guess for the area (its slope is \ln x + 1)


-x
Removes the extra +1 from that slope





6. Step
H(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ 1 & x \ge 0 \end{cases} \qquad H' = \delta, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{x} H = \max(0, x)







Part
Meaning




H(x)
Step: off before 0, on from 0


\delta
Delta: zero everywhere except a spike at 0 with total area 1


\max(0, x)
Ramp: flat until 0, then rises with slope 1

title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
Six rules of differentiation









Item and key formula
Example
Application




1. Sum\left(\sum_i c_i f_i\right)' = \sum_i c_i f_i'
(3x^2 + 5\sin x)' = \mathbf{6x + 5\cos x}
Derivative of a total cost or weighted score, e.g. w_1 a + w_2 b


2. Product(fg)' = f'g + fg'
(x^2 \sin x)' = \mathbf{2x \sin x + x^2 \cos x}
Revenue = price × quantity (both changing); power = voltage × current


3. Quotient\left(\tfrac{f}{g}\right)' = \tfrac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}
\left(\tfrac{\sin x}{x}\right)' = \tfrac{x\cos x - \sin x}{x^2}
Rates and ratios: cost per unit, efficiency, utilization = busy time / total time


4. Chain\tfrac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\,g'(x)
\tfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = \mathbf{2x\cos(x^2)}(outer derivative × inner derivative)
Backpropagation in neural networks; related rates (balloon radius as air is pumped in)


5. Inverse(f^{-1})'(y) = \tfrac{1}{f'(x)}, y = f(x), f'(x) \ne 0
y = e^x,\ x = \ln y \to \tfrac{dx}{dy} = \tfrac{1}{e^x} = \tfrac{1}{y}(this proves (\ln y)' = 1/y)
Derivatives of \ln, \arcsin, \sqrt{\phantom{x}}; converting “time per task” ↔︎ “tasks per time”


6. L’Hôpital\lim\limits_{x\to a} \tfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\to a} \tfrac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}for 0/0 or \infty/\infty, if the right-hand limit exists
\lim\limits_{x\to0} \tfrac{\sin x}{x} = \tfrac{\cos 0}{1} = \mathbf{1}\lim\limits_{x\to0} \tfrac{e^x - 1}{x} = \tfrac{e^0}{1} = \mathbf{1}
Limits that look like 0/0: continuous compounding → e^x; edge-case behavior of algorithms





Theorem formulation


1. Sum
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i f_i\right)' = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i f_i'







Part
Meaning




f_i
One of the functions added together


c_i
Constant weight, carried through unchanged


f_i'
Slope of that function on its own


\sum_{i=1}^{n}
Add up all n terms: slopes add just as the functions do





2. Product
(fg)' = f'g + fg'



Part
Meaning




f'g
Change from f moving while g stays still


fg'
Change from g moving while f stays still


+
Total change is the two added together





3. Quotient
\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}, \qquad g \ne 0



Part
Meaning




f'g
Top grows, so the ratio rises


-fg'
Bottom grows, so the ratio falls


g^2
Scales the change by the size of the bottom, squared


g \ne 0
The ratio must exist at that point





4. Chain
\frac{d}{dx} f\bigl(g(x)\bigr) = f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,g'(x)



Part
Meaning




g(x)
Inner function, worked out first


f
Outer function, applied to the result


f'(g(x))
Outer slope, measured at the inner value (not at x)


g'(x)
Inner slope: how fast the input to f is moving





5. Inverse
(f^{-1})'(y) = \frac{1}{f'(x)}, \qquad y = f(x)



Part
Meaning




f^{-1}
Inverse function: takes y back to x


f'(x)
Slope of the original, at the x that gave y


\tfrac{1}{f'(x)}
Rise and run swap, so the slope flips


f'(x) \ne 0
Needed: a flat spot would make the inverse vertical





6. L’Hôpital
\lim_{x\to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}







Part
Meaning




a
The point approached (may be \pm\infty)


\tfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}
A ratio that heads to 0/0 or \infty/\infty; otherwise the rule does not apply


\tfrac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}
Ratio of the slopes, each differentiated separately (not the quotient rule)


g'(x) \ne 0
Needed near a, and the right-hand limit must exist

title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
Six theorems









Item and key formula
Example
Application




1. Fundamental TheoremIf f(x) = \int_a^x s(t)\,dt then f' = s;\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)
\int_0^3 2x\,dx = 3^2 - 0^2 = \mathbf{9} (no Riemann sums)\tfrac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \cos t\,dt = \mathbf{\cos x}
Velocity → distance; flow rate → total volume; demand rate → cumulative demand; PDF → CDF


2. Max–min / intermediate valuef continuous on [a, b]:f(m) \le f(x) \le f(M) for all x, and f(c) = N for every N between f(m) and f(M)
x^2 on [-1, 2]: max \mathbf{4} at x = 2, min \mathbf{0} at x = 0Counterexample: the step on [-1, 1] never equals 0.5 (not continuous)
Guarantees an optimum exists (basis of optimization); justifies bisection root-finding


3. Mean ValueIf f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then f'(c) = \tfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} for some c in (a, b)
x^2 on [0, 2]: average slope = 4/2 = 2; f'(c) = 2c = 2 \to \mathbf{c = 1}Drive 120 km in 2 h → at some instant exactly 60 km/h
Average-speed cameras; proving error bounds for numerical methods


4. Taylor seriesf(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \tfrac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n
e^x \approx 1 + x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} \to at x = 0.1: \mathbf{1.105} (true 1.10517)\sin x \approx x - \tfrac{x^3}{6}
How calculators compute \sin, e^x, \sqrt{\phantom{x}}; \sin\theta \approx \theta for pendulums; gradient descent / Newton’s method


5. Taylor remainderR_n(x) = \tfrac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}, c between a and x
e^x at x = 0.1, n = 2: error = \tfrac{e^c}{6}\cdot 0.001, between 0.000167 and 0.000184Actual error 0.000171 ✓
Knowing how accurate an approximation is; choosing step size or number of terms in solvers


6. Binomial(1+x)^p = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty} \tbinom{p}{k} x^k, \lvert x \rvert < 1
p = 2: 1 + 2x + x^2 (stops)p = \tfrac12: \sqrt{1.1} \approx 1 + 0.05 - 0.00125 = \mathbf{1.04875} (true 1.04881)p = -1: 1 - x + x^2 - \dots (never stops)
Quick approximations, e.g. (1+r)^n \approx 1 + nr; relativity \gamma \approx 1 + \tfrac{v^2}{2c^2}; binomial distribution





Theorem formulation


1. Fundamental Theorem
\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x s(t)\,dt = s(x), \qquad \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)



Part
Meaning




s(t)
Rate (speed) at moment t; continuous


\int_a^x s(t)\,dt
Amount collected from a up to x


\tfrac{d}{dx}
Slope of that amount, which gives the rate back


f'(x)\,dx
One tiny step of change


f(b) - f(a)
Total change: end minus start





2. Max–min / intermediate value
f(m) \le f(x) \le f(M), \qquad f(c) = N







Part
Meaning




[a, b]
Closed interval: both ends are included


continuous f
No jumps; without it both claims can fail


f(m),\ f(M)
Lowest and highest values, reached at points m and M


N
Any value between the lowest and the highest


c
A point where the function equals N (there may be several)





3. Mean Value
f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}







Part
Meaning




f(b) - f(a)
Total change in value


b - a
Length of the interval


\tfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}
Average slope, the line joining the two ends


f'(c)
Slope at one single point


c
Some point strictly between a and b; the theorem says it exists, not where


continuous on [a, b]
No jumps, the ends included


differentiable on (a, b)
A slope at every inside point. \lvert x \rvert on [-1, 1] has a corner at 0: its average slope is 0, but it never has slope 0





4. Taylor series
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n







Part
Meaning




f(a)
Value of the function at the point a (the n = 0 term)


f'(a)
Rate of change, the slope


f''(a)
Curvature: how the slope bends


f^{(n)}(a)
Behavior of the function at higher order n


(x-a)^n
Distance from the point being approximated to a, at order n


n!
Normalizes the coefficient: n derivatives of (x-a)^n give n!


\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
Add every order; equals f(x) where the remainder goes to 0





5. Taylor remainder
R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}







Part
Meaning




R_n(x)
Error left after stopping at order n


f^{(n+1)}(c)
The next derivative, taken at c instead of a


c
Unknown point between a and x; bound the error with the worst case


(n+1)!
Grows fast, so more terms shrink the error


(x-a)^{n+1}
Distance: the error is small close to a





6. Binomial
(1+x)^p = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \binom{p}{k} x^k, \qquad \binom{p}{k} = \frac{1}{k!}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(p-j)







Part
Meaning




p
Any power: whole, fraction or negative


\tbinom{p}{k}
Weight of the x^k term


\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(p-j)
Multiply k factors, starting at p and dropping by one each time; hits 0 when p is a whole number below k, so the series stops


k!
Normalizes the coefficient, as in Taylor series


\lvert x \rvert < 1
Needed for the endless sum to settle (not when the series stops)

title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
The big picture
The functions describe how things behave (growth, cycles, switches); the rules let you differentiate complex models built from those pieces; the theorems guarantee that optimization and approximation actually work.
